summaries.example: Imagine a toy world made of tiny dots. Each dot has simple features, such as a color or mass, and dots have places and distances from one another. Lewis asks whether everything else—chairs, storms, causes, and even what could happen—can be understood from these basic facts. For possibilities, he might compare you with a very similar person in another possible world. That person would be your counterpart.
summaries.summary: David Lewis’s metaphysics is a large plan for understanding reality. Metaphysics asks what exists and what those things are like. Lewis thinks a good theory should fit together what common sense and science suggest, while remaining clear and economical. He gives special attention to basic entities, basic properties and relations, and possible worlds. On his view, many facts about ordinary objects, causes, laws, and minds might be explained from more basic facts. He also develops counterpart theory: when we say that someone could have been different, we may mean that a suitably similar person exists in another possible world. Lewis’s views are powerful but debated, especially because some philosophers think basic reality must include facts about possibility or kinds of properties that Lewis tries to explain in other ways.
key_ideas: Lewis thinks metaphysics asks very broad questions: What exists, and what is everything like?
He tries to connect ordinary things and big ideas to a basic description of reality.
His idea of possible worlds helps explain possibility and necessity.
His method balances common sense, science, arguments, and the wish for a simple theory.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lewis shows how one picture of reality can guide many areas of philosophy. His ideas encourage us to ask what is basic, what can be explained by something else, and how science should influence metaphysics. They also show why a small change in how we understand “could have happened” can affect questions about people, objects, time, causes, and laws of nature.

important_terms.definition: The study of what exists and what the things that exist are like.
A property or relation that belongs to the basic structure of reality, rather than being built from something more basic.
A way of saying that one set of facts fixes another set of facts, even if the second set is not directly mentioned.
A similar person or thing in another possible world used to explain what could have happened to someone or something.

questions_to_think_about: If a thing is made of smaller parts, are the parts more basic than the whole?
Could a person have lived a very different life and still been that person?
Would two worlds be different if their basic dots and features were arranged differently?

summaries.example: Suppose we ask, “Could this particular bicycle have had a different chain?” Lewis’s counterpart theory does not require the very same bicycle to exist in two worlds. Instead, it looks for a bicycle in another possible world that resembles the actual bicycle in the respects important to the discussion. A counterpart may have a different chain while remaining similar enough to count as representing what could have happened to the original bicycle. Because similarity can be weighted differently, the answer may depend on whether shape, origin, parts, or some other feature matters most.
summaries.summary: The entry presents David Lewis’s metaphysics as a systematic attempt to answer two questions: what exists and what reality is like. Lewis’s inquiry is holistic: it begins with beliefs supplied by common sense and science and seeks a well-organized equilibrium rather than deriving everything from a single unquestioned foundation. The resulting program concerns fundamental ontology, modality, and reductions of less-basic facts. A simplified Lewisian picture treats basic particulars as simples or spacetime points, characterized by perfectly natural properties and relations. These properties are intended to be minimal, non-modal, and intrinsic, while empirical science—especially fundamental physics—helps determine which ones there are. Lewis’s Humean Supervenience says, roughly, that no worlds differ in total truth without differing in basic distributions across spacetime, but the entry distinguishes this supervenience claim from the stronger claim that all other facts reduce to those facts. Lewis also allows qualifications about quantum physics, possible non-spatiotemporal natural relations, and the possibility of gunk. In counterpart theory, modal claims about an individual are analyzed using suitable counterparts in other worlds, with similarity standards that may be context-sensitive. The theory offers solutions to puzzles about essential properties, changing parts, fission, and trans-world identity, while generating disputes about logic and the nature of similarity.
key_ideas: Lewis treats metaphysics as factual inquiry into reality, not merely analysis of language or concepts.
His program has three connected parts: fundamental ontology, an account of modality, and reductions of less-basic facts.
Perfectly natural properties and relations are meant to provide a minimal, non-modal basis for describing reality, though the source notes important qualifications from physics.

Humean Supervenience is weaker than reduction: it says that certain differences require differences in basic arrangements, not necessarily that all higher-level facts can be explicitly reduced to them.
Lewis remains cautious about whether the basic entities are only spacetime points, whether reality is composed entirely of simples, and whether only spatiotemporal relations are natural.
Counterpart theory explains de re modal claims through relevant similarity rather than strict identity across possible worlds; the relevant similarity can vary by context.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lewis’s work illustrates how metaphysical commitments can shape accounts of causation, persistence, laws, mind, and modality. It also raises a central methodological question: should philosophy seek a compact fundamental description modeled partly on science, or should it treat possibilities and necessities as basic? Counterpart theory is important because it replaces strict identity across worlds with a flexible representational relation, making room for multiple, asymmetric, and context-sensitive comparisons while also challenging familiar principles of modal logic.

important_terms.definition: The branch of philosophy concerned with what exists and with the general nature of reality.
A property or relation whose pattern among fundamental entities helps determine the basic structure of reality; Lewis treats naturalness as objective and potentially graded.
The view that differences in all facts require differences in the distribution of basic qualities or relations across spacetime; Lewis accepts, at most, a contingent version.
The claim that facts about possibility and necessity can be analyzed without treating modal notions as fundamental.
An individual or object in another possible world that resembles an actual individual in contextually relevant respects and represents what could have happened to it.
A fact or feature that concerns what something is like in itself, independently of distinct things; Lewis connects intrinsic nature with natural properties.
A particular with no proper parts, discussed as a possible candidate for the basic constituents of reality.
A theory of inquiry that seeks a coherent fit among common-sense beliefs, scientific beliefs, arguments, and standards of theoretical success.

questions_to_think_about: Is a theory more successful if it uses fewer basic kinds of entities and properties, or can simplicity leave out something important?
Does a difference in basic physical arrangement really determine every difference in laws, causation, minds, or values?
If counterpart relations depend on context, does that make modal truth subjective, or can the facts still be objective?
Should the nature of possibility be explained from non-modal facts, or should some modal features be fundamental?
What should metaphysics do when its preferred picture is challenged by developments in physics?

summaries.example: Think about a school robotics club’s “same robot” question. One robot could have been built with a different wheel or battery. Lewis’s counterpart theory says we need not imagine the actual robot appearing in two worlds. Instead, another-world robot can count as its counterpart if it resembles the actual one in the important ways. If we care most about the robot’s design, a robot with a new battery may qualify. If we care most about its original parts, it may not. The theory explains why answers about what a thing could have been can depend on the comparison we are making.
summaries.summary: David Lewis’s metaphysics asks two very broad questions: what exists, and what are those things like? He treats these as questions about reality itself. His method is not to begin with one final list of basic commitments and force every other belief to follow. Instead, he tries to bring common sense, science, arguments, and standards of simplicity into a coherent overall view. The entry focuses mainly on his fundamental ontology. Lewis thinks a serious ontology includes not only particular things but also properties and relations, some of which are more natural than others. Perfectly natural features are supposed to mark the basic joints of reality. A simplified version of his view describes basic particulars, their natural properties, and their relations, with other facts explained from them. Humean Supervenience is closely related: it says that worlds cannot differ in their total facts without differing in basic arrangements of qualities and spacetime relations. However, supervenience is weaker than reduction, and Lewis treats his official version as contingent. The entry also explains counterpart theory. Rather than saying that the same ordinary object exists as a part of many possible worlds, Lewis says that claims about what an object could have been involve suitable counterparts in other worlds. Similarity can depend on what matters in the context, which helps explain disagreements about essential properties but also creates logical and philosophical challenges.
key_ideas: Lewis sees metaphysics as an investigation of reality, not just a study of how people use words.
He tries to build a unified system that respects both common sense and science.
His basic picture gives a central role to fundamental entities, natural properties, and relations among them.
Humean Supervenience links differences between worlds to differences in their basic arrangements, but it is not exactly the same as full reduction.
Lewis’s account of possibility uses possible worlds and, for particular objects, counterparts rather than strict identity across worlds.
Critics question whether basic properties can really be non-modal and intrinsic, and whether the theory fits what physics tells us.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lewis provides a model of ambitious, systematic philosophy. His approach connects questions about the basic furniture of reality with questions about possibility, identity, causation, laws, and persistence. The debates matter because they concern what explanation should look like: whether higher-level truths are fixed by a physical base, whether possibility can be explained without primitive possibility, and whether flexible similarity gives a better account of modal claims than strict identity across worlds.

important_terms.definition: The study of reality at the most general level, including what exists and what its basic features are.
A property or relation treated as part of nature’s basic structure, rather than as something fully explained by more basic features.
The idea that a change in any facts requires a change in the arrangement of basic qualities or relations at spacetime locations.
The philosophical idea that one kind of fact can be explained in terms of another, less basic kind of fact.
An object in another possible world that resembles an actual object in the respects that matter for a particular claim about possibility.
A world that is different from ours but is considered as a way reality could have been.

questions_to_think_about: What makes one fact more basic than another: its simplicity, its role in science, or something else?
If two worlds have the same basic arrangement, could they still differ in laws or mental facts?
When deciding what you could have done, which similarities to your actual self should matter most?
Can a theory be objective if the relevant comparison standards sometimes depend on context?
Why might someone prefer counterparts to saying that one object literally exists in several worlds?
